title: Merino heirloom shawl
subtitle: An openwork treble lace triangle with a picot border in fingering-weight merino, after Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: This triangular shawl uses an openwork treble lace body worked from the top centre to 155 cm wide and 72 cm deep, finishing with a two-round picot border. The fabric is worked in fingering-weight merino on a 3.25 mm hook. The pattern is adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet and requires confidence with counting open-lace rows and maintaining consistent tension.
sourceNotes: Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), triangular lace shawl with picot border (Internet Archive, archive.org). Openwork lace structure confirmed against Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet lace chapter.
heroPrompt: A fine triangular crochet shawl in ivory fingering-weight merino, fully blocked and pinned out on a dark wood table, showing the openwork treble lace body and the picot border along both diagonal edges.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fabric where stitches are deliberately spaced apart using chain bars between groups of trebles, producing a net-like structure that shows through to the layer beneath.

The unit of stitches that tiles across a row to produce the lace pattern. In this shawl each repeat is 4 stitches wide (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr separated by a ch-2 space). The repeat count increases by one on each shell row.
A finishing border where a small ch-3 loop is secured with a slip stitch, producing a toothed decorative edge. In lace shawls the picot is placed at every chain space along the diagonal edges.

content.text: This shawl is based on a triangular lace construction published in Weldon's Practical Crochet in 1890. The body is an
openwork lace
worked in pairs of trebles separated by ch-2 bars, with ch-2 spaces between each pair. The triangle grows from a central chain ring, adding one
lace repeat
at each edge on every other row. A two-round
picot border
finishes the two diagonal edges.

This is an advanced pattern. The lace structure requires accurate stitch counting on every row: a missed chain space or an extra treble shifts all subsequent repeats. Work in good light and check the count after every increase row. Fingering-weight merino benefits considerably from wet blocking, which opens the chain bars and sets the lace structure firmly.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 300 g fingering-weight merino yarn (4-ply). A 3.25 mm crochet hook (US D/3). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (at least 2). Blocking mat. Rust-proof blocking pins. Tape measure.

content.text: Gauge

24 tr x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight merino with a 3.25 mm hook, measured over plain treble fabric after blocking. Lace gauge opens up with blocking, so measure the swatch after a full wet block rather than before. The finished shawl dimensions depend on both pre-block tension and the thoroughness of blocking.
Stitches used
chain (ch): UK and US shared.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
picot: ch 3, sl st into base of chain.
Pattern

The shawl is worked flat in rows. The lace repeat is: 2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr (V-pair), ch 2 between each V-pair. The central spine on odd rows is a ch-4 loop; on even rows it is a (2 tr, ch 4, 2 tr) unit. Place a stitch marker in the central chain on every row and move it up each row.
Foundation ring
Ch 8. Sl st to form a ring.
Row 1 (right side)
Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). 2 tr in ring. Ch 4 (centre loop, mark it). 2 tr in ring. Ch 2. 1 tr in ring. Turn. (7 tr, 2 ch-2 spaces, 1 ch-4 centre loop)
Row 2 (increase row)

Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). 2 tr in first ch-2 space. Ch 2. Into the ch-4 centre loop work: 2 tr, ch 4 (move marker), 2 tr. Ch 2. 2 tr in last ch-2 space. Ch 2. 1 tr in 3rd ch of turning ch. Turn. (15 tr, 4 ch-2 spaces, 1 ch-4 centre loop)
Row 3 (increase row)

Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). *2 tr in next ch-2 space. Ch 2*; repeat from * to * to the ch-4 centre loop. Into the ch-4 loop work: 2 tr, ch 4 (move marker), 2 tr. Ch 2. *2 tr in next ch-2 space. Ch 2*; repeat from * to * to end. 1 tr in 3rd ch of turning ch. Turn. (one V-pair added at each edge)
Rows 4 to approximately 86

Repeat Row 3 on every row. Each row adds one V-pair at each edge. After approximately 86 rows the widest row contains approximately 43 V-pairs on each side of the centre loop, giving a width of 155 cm and depth of 72 cm after blocking. Check the width against the gauge measurement after blocking a swatch before committing to the final row count.

attrs.title: Counting the row
attrs.body: At the end of each row the stitch count should be: (row number x 4) + 3. After Row 10 you should have 43 stitches, not counting chains. If the count is off by more than 2, count back through the row to find where a space was skipped or an extra stitch was added.

content.text: Picot border

Round 1: join yarn at the top right corner. Work 1 dc into each stitch or chain along the top straight edge. At corners work (1 dc, ch 2, 1 dc). Continue down the right diagonal edge and up the left diagonal edge, working 1 dc into each row-end tr and 1 dc into each chain space along the edges. Join with sl st.

Round 2 (picot): *1 dc in next dc. Ch 3. Sl st into base of ch (picot made). 1 dc in each of next 2 dc*; repeat from * to * around the two diagonal edges only. At the bottom point work (1 dc, picot, 1 dc) into the corner ch-2 space. Fasten off.
Finishing

Fasten off and weave in all ends. Wet-block thoroughly: soak in cool water for at least 15 minutes to allow full saturation, press out excess water in a towel (do not wring), then pin out on a blocking mat to the stated dimensions. Pin the top edge straight, place pins at the two top corners and the bottom point, then pin along both diagonal edges at 5 cm intervals, easing the lace open. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.
Care
Handwash in cool water with a wool-specific wash. Handle gently when wet. Lay flat to dry away from direct heat. The lace structure holds its shape best if re-pinned lightly after each wash.
What to try next

The same V-pair lace structure works as a rectangular stole: cast on a fixed number of repeats and work straight rows without the central spine increase. A deeper picot of ch 5 gives a longer tooth on the border. For a finer piece, lace-weight yarn on a 2.75 mm hook produces a cobweb-weight shawl in the same construction.
